headline: People are talking less every year

sources.title: A quiet crisis? Study finds people are speaking far less (Ynet)
Are we talking less? A Q&A with psychologist Matthias Mehl (University of Arizona)
We're losing 338 spoken words every day (BBC Science Focus)
Are We Speaking Less Than Ever? (video, The Social CTV)

chunks.text: How many words do you say in a day? Fewer than your parents did, and far [[fewer]] than people twenty years ago. A new [[study]] in the [[journal]] Perspectives on Psychological Science found that the [[average]] person spoke about 16,000 words a day in the mid-2000s. As the years {{went by}}, people talked less and less. By 2019, the number had {{dropped off}} to about 12,000, a fall of nearly 28 percent. On average, people lost about 338 [[spoken words]] from their daily talk every year.

verbs.wrong: To slow to a complete stop
verbs.why: Weeks go by, seasons go by, and whole decades go by faster than we expect. As the years went by, people simply said less and less.

verbs.wrong: To be counted one by one
verbs.why: Ticket sales drop off after opening week, and visits drop off in winter. Daily spoken words dropped off from 16,000 to about 12,000.

chunks.text: The [[researchers]] did not {{set out}} to study [[silence]]. They combined 22 older studies from 2005 to 2019, covering about 2,200 [[volunteers]] aged 10 to 94 in the United States, Europe, and Australia. In those studies, people wore small [[recorders]] that captured short moments of sound during the day. Because the recordings were made for other research questions, nobody changed their [[behavior]]. Scientists are still trying to {{figure out}} what the numbers mean, but the [[pattern]] is clear, and it is strongest in people under 25.

verbs.correct: To begin with a clear goal
verbs.why: Explorers set out to cross oceans, and startups set out to change an industry. These researchers set out to study other topics and found the silence by accident.

verbs.correct: To find the reason for something
verbs.why: Mechanics figure out why engines fail, and parents figure out why a baby keeps waking up at night. Scientists are still working to figure out why we all talk less.

chunks.text: Where did the words go? Think about a normal day. We {{type out}} messages instead of calling. We {{check out}} at the store without a word to a [[cashier]]. We order food in an app and follow a map's quiet [[directions]] instead of asking a [[stranger]] for help. One by one, we have {{cut out}} the [[small conversations]] that once filled a day, and the [[habit]] of [[chatting]] with strangers is slowly {{dying out}}.

verbs.correct: To write a message with a keyboard
verbs.wrong: To read a long message twice
verbs.why: People type out long birthday wishes and type out complaints to airlines. We now type out words we once would have spoken.

verbs.correct: To pay and leave a store
verbs.wrong: To wait in a longer line
verbs.why: Shoppers check out at the machines near the door, and a customer with one item can check out in under a minute at the pharmacy. Millions now check out without a single word to anyone.

verbs.correct: To remove something from your life
verbs.why: Doctors tell patients to cut out salt, and savers cut out small daily purchases. One by one, we have cut out the little chats that filled a day.
Old customs die out, and languages die out when children stop learning them. The habit of chatting with strangers is slowly dying out.

chunks.text: Why does it matter? The scientists warn that people who talk less may {{miss out}} on [[connection]], at a time when many countries already worry about [[loneliness]]. A text message cannot copy the [[tone]], timing, and [[warmth]] of a voice. Some good [[advice]] is simple and free. {{Strike up}} a conversation while you wait [[in line]] for coffee. Call an old friend to {{catch up}}. In a world that is slowly going quiet, the healthiest thing you can do may be to {{speak up}}.

verbs.correct: To lose the chance to enjoy something
verbs.wrong: To arrive too early for a party
verbs.why: Late shoppers miss out on the best deals, and busy workers miss out on family dinners. People who talk less may miss out on real connection.
Travelers strike up conversations on trains, and neighbors strike up friendships over the fence. One easy step is to strike up a chat while you wait in line.

verbs.correct: To share news with a friend
verbs.wrong: To cancel plans at the last minute
verbs.why: Old classmates catch up over coffee, and cousins catch up at weddings. Calling a friend to catch up is one easy way to talk more.

verbs.correct: To talk instead of staying quiet
verbs.why: Shy students learn to speak up in class, and workers speak up in meetings. In a quieter world, the healthiest choice may be to speak up.

mainIdea.s: A large study found people now speak thousands of words fewer each day than twenty years ago. Scientists worry the loss of small conversations may deepen loneliness around the world.
mainIdea.why: Daily spoken words fell about 28 percent from the mid-2000s to 2019, and researchers link talking with connection.

mainIdea.s: Researchers reported that we speak far fewer words daily and proved that smartphones alone are the cause. They say the decline stops as soon as people delete their social apps.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the researchers say the cause is not proven, and nothing in the study shows that deleting apps stops the decline.

mainIdea.s: A new report found that people are speaking more than ever but listening far less than before. Experts blame noisy offices and recommend daily quiet hours in every workplace.
mainIdea.why: The study measured the opposite trend. People are speaking less each year, and offices were not blamed.

tf.s: Daily spoken words dropped off from about 16,000 to about 12,000.
tf.why: That is a fall of nearly 28 percent between the mid-2000s and 2019.

tf.s: The researchers combined 22 older studies from 2010 to 2019.
tf.why: They combined 22 older studies from 2005 to 2019, about 2,200 volunteers aged 10 to 94, to figure out why daily talk has dropped off.

tf.s: The decline is strongest in people under 25.
tf.why: Younger people are cutting out spoken conversation faster than older adults.

tf.s: The recorders captured every word the volunteers said all day.
tf.why: The small recorders captured only short moments of sound, so the researchers had to figure out daily totals from samples.

tf.s: The volunteers were told to talk less for the study.
tf.why: The researchers did not set out to study silence. The recordings were made for other research questions, so nobody changed their behavior.

tf.s: The scientists warn that talking less may mean missing out on connection.
tf.why: They point to loneliness, and note that texts cannot copy the tone and warmth of a voice.

lines.text: There's a study that says the whole world is going quiet. The average person spoke about 16,000 words a day in the mid-2000s, and by 2019 it had {{dropped off}} to around 12,000.
That's more than a quarter of our words gone. [[I'm speechless]]. Which, apparently, is the trend anyway.
Nearly 28 percent, and it wasn't sudden. As the years {{went by}}, people lost about 338 spoken words a day, every single year.
Hold on. How do you even count that? Did they follow people around with a notebook?
Recorders. About 2,200 volunteers, aged 10 to 94, wore little devices that captured short bits of sound during the day. And the researchers never {{set out}} to measure talking at all.
So they were studying something else and the silence was just there in the data. That [[speaks volumes]].
It does, because nobody changed their behavior for the recordings. The scientists still can't {{figure out}} exactly why it's happening, but the drop is strongest in people under 25.
I could have told them that for free. I {{type out}} twenty messages before I say good morning to anyone.
And it doesn't stop there. You {{check out}} at the store without a word, the app orders your lunch, the map tells you where to turn.
And we used to ask a stranger for directions. One by one we've {{cut out}} every little chat.

That's the worry. The habit of chatting with strangers is {{dying out}}, and the scientists say people who talk less may {{miss out}} on real connection. A text can't carry the tone or the warmth of a voice.
[[Actions speak louder than words]], and here the action is nobody talking. Do they have a fix, or just the bad news?
Nothing official. But the simple fix is free. {{Strike up}} a conversation while you wait in line for coffee. Call an old friend and {{catch up}}.
[[Say no more]]. I owe my sister a phone call, and she knows it.
Then {{speak up}}. The world is going quiet, so somebody has to.
[[Loud and clear]]. She's getting all 338 of my missing words.

expressions.def: Used when something is so surprising or shocking that you cannot think of what to say
ex: They gave me the award? I'm speechless.
He sold the house without telling her. I'm speechless.

expressions.def: Shows or reveals a lot about a situation, even without anyone saying it directly
ex: He didn't come to the party, and that speaks volumes.
The empty parking lot speaks volumes about how the restaurant is doing.

expressions.def: What people do matters more than what they say
ex: He keeps promising to help, but actions speak louder than words.
She didn't say sorry, she just fixed it. Actions speak louder than words.

expressions.def: Used to show you already understand and agree, so the other person does not need to explain further
ex: You want to leave before the speeches start? Say no more.
Free pizza at the meeting? Say no more, I'm there.

expressions.def: Used to say that you have understood a message completely
ex: Turn the music down? Loud and clear.
The boss said no more late reports, and everyone heard it loud and clear.
